Package org.aristonis.diwan.database.query

Class QueryGrammar

java.lang.Object
org.aristonis.diwan.database.query.QueryGrammar
Direct Known Subclasses:
PostgresQueryGrammar, SQLiteQueryGrammar
public abstract class QueryGrammar extends Object
Compiles a Builder into SQL for one database, a hand port of Laravel's Illuminate\Database\Query\Grammars\Grammar and the quoting helpers of its parent Illuminate\Database\Grammar.

The base class writes Laravel's generic SQL. Each database module extends it and overrides the compile and where methods its database writes differently. Laravel dispatches a where clause by building a method name from a string; here compileWhere(Builder, Where) branches on the Where type, and each branch calls a protected method with Laravel's name, which is the method to override.

A grammar is built for one table prefix, the prefix of the connection it serves, and adds it to every table name it writes. Instances hold no other state and are safe to share between threads, unless a subclass says otherwise.

Implementation Requirements:
Every value is written as ? through parameter(Object) unless it is an Expression, and every identifier is quoted through wrap(Object) or wrapTable(Object). An override must keep both rules: they are what keeps user input out of the SQL text. Methods added in later versions come with a body, so existing grammars keep compiling.

      public String compileSelect(Builder query)

      Throws:

    • compileInsert

      public Optional<String> compileInsert(Builder query, List<? extends Map<String,?>> rows)
      Compiles an insert of one or more rows.

      With one row, columns follow the row's key order. With several, columns are sorted by name, as Laravel's builder sorts each row's keys before an insert of many rows. Every row's values are written in the column order; bind them the same way, as insertColumns(List) returns it. One empty row inserts the defaults. Laravel compiles any mismatch of keys into SQL whose bindings no longer line up; here it is refused.

      Parameters:
      query - the query, never null, with a table
      rows - the rows, never null; each a map of column to value, where an Expression is written as given
      Returns:
      the SQL, or empty if there are no rows and nothing should run
      Throws:
      NullPointerException - if an argument or row is null
      IllegalArgumentException - if the rows do not all have the same keys, or more than one row is empty

    • prepareBindingsForUpdate

      public List<Object> prepareBindingsForUpdate(Builder query, Map<String,?> values)
      Orders the bindings of an update of this query: the new values first, in column order, then the buckets the compiled statement writes, except select. Laravel's base grammar puts the join bindings first, because its joined update writes the joins before set; the SQLite and PostgreSQL rewrites put the joins in a subquery after set, so they come after the values here. The buckets are every one but select when writesFullSelect(org.aristonis.diwan.database.query.Builder) is true, otherwise from, join and where only, since a plain update ... set ... where writes no group, having, order or union clause.
      Parameters:
      query - the query, never null
      values - the columns and new values, never null; Expression values are skipped, a Builder value contributes its own bindings in its place
      Returns:
      the bindings, unmodifiable, never null
      Throws:
      NullPointerException - if an argument is null

    • prepareBindingsForDelete

      public List<Object> prepareBindingsForDelete(Builder query)
      Orders the bindings of a delete of this query: the buckets the compiled statement writes, except select, in BindingType order. A delete has no new values, so no value bindings come first, unlike prepareBindingsForUpdate(Builder, Map).
      Parameters:

      Returns:
      the bindings, unmodifiable, never null
      Throws:

      the converted bindings, unmodifiable, never null

      NullPointerException - if bindings is null

    • substituteBindingsIntoRawSql

      public String substituteBindingsIntoRawSql(String sql, List<?> bindings)
      Writes bindings into SQL as escaped literals, for display and logging only.

      The result must never be run. Literals assume standard SQL strings, where a backslash is an ordinary character, as on SQLite and on PostgreSQL with standard_conforming_strings on; escaping is in any case weaker than binding.

      Each ? outside a string literal and outside a quoted identifier takes the next binding. Inside a '...' literal or a "..." identifier, a ? stays and the other quote character is plain text; a doubled quote ('' or "") stays inside its region. Laravel tracks only string literals, so a quoted name holding ? or ' is substituted into or ends the scan in the wrong state. A doubled ?? is kept as written. A ? without a binding left stays as ?. Laravel also skips a backslash-escaped quote, which only MySQL reads that way; this grammar does so only when isBackslashEscape() says its database does, since otherwise a literal ending in a backslash would hide every later placeholder.

      Parameters:
      sql - the SQL, never null
      bindings - the bindings, already prepared, never null
      Returns:
      the SQL with literals, never null
      Throws:
      NullPointerException - if an argument is null
      IllegalArgumentException - if a string binding holds a NUL character
      UnsupportedOperationException - if a binding cannot be written as a literal

    • isBackslashEscape

      protected boolean isBackslashEscape()
      Returns whether this grammar's database reads \' inside a string literal as an escaped quote.
      Returns:
      true if a backslash escapes a quote
      Implementation Requirements:
      The base returns false: standard SQL, SQLite and PostgreSQL with standard strings treat a backslash as an ordinary character.

      protected String compileUpdateWithJoins(Builder query, String table, String columns, String where)
      Compiles an update of a query with joins. Laravel's base grammar writes update t inner join ... set ..., which neither SQLite nor PostgreSQL accept, and which would need the join bindings before the set values; here the base grammar refuses it and a database grammar rewrites the query, keeping the order of prepareBindingsForUpdate(org.aristonis.diwan.database.query.Builder, java.util.Map<java.lang.String, ?>): set values, then join, then where.
      Parameters:
      query - the query, never null
      table - the wrapped table, never null
      columns - the compiled set list, never null
      where - the compiled where clause, never null, may be empty
      Returns:
      the SQL, never null
      Throws:
      UnsupportedOperationException - always, in the base grammar

    • eagerKeyChunkSize

      public int eagerKeyChunkSize()
      Returns how many keys an eager load binds in one query; a longer key list runs in chunks.

      The default of 900 keeps a query under the 999 bindings of older SQLite builds, such as Android's, with room for the bindings of an eager constraint. A grammar overrides it for a database that allows more.

      Returns:
      the number of bound keys per query, at least 1

    • inlineKeyChunkSize

      public int inlineKeyChunkSize()
      Returns how many integer keys an eager load writes into one query's SQL; a longer key list runs in chunks.

      Inlined keys take no binding, so this limit guards the length of the statement instead: 20,000 keys of at most 20 characters each, with their separators, stay well under SQLite's default maximum of 1,000,000 bytes.

      Returns:
      the number of inlined keys per query, at least 1
